chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, all from Ibn Mahbub from Hisham ibn Salim from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I was present when asked about a man who sold a virgin slave-girl to another man for a period of one year. When the buyer took possession of her, he freed her the next day, married her, and made her manumission her dowry. Then he died a month later.
Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'If the one who bought her for a year had wealth or a guarantee that covered the debt owed in her neck, then his manumission and his marriage were valid.'

He said: 'And if the one who bought her, freed her, and married her had no wealth or guarantee on the day he died that covered the debt owed in her neck, then his manumission and his marriage are invalid, because he freed what he did not own, and I consider that she remains in slavery for her first master.'
It was said to him: 'If she conceived from the one who freed her and married her, what is the status of what is in her womb?' He said: 'It follows its mother in her condition.'

key_terms.رَقَبَتِهَا: In her neck (referring to the debt/price owed for her)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a slave-girl's manumission and marriage if the buyer dies without paying off her debt?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the fiqh of *kitabah* (manumission by installment) by establishing that the buyer's solvency at the time of death determines the validity of his prior manumission and marriage contracts. If he lacked sufficient assets to cover the remaining debt, his acts are deemed invalid because he effectively manumitted what he did not fully own, causing the slave-girl to revert to the first master. The ruling also clarifies that any offspring from this union follows the mother's status, reinforcing the principle of *al-walad li-l-firash* in the context of conditional ownership.
